title: Canada Rewrites Citizenship Rules for Generations Born Abroad
excerpt: Bill C-3, now in force, ends the first-generation limit and automatically restores citizenship to thousands cut off by outdated law.
body:
Canada's government made a sweeping change to who counts as a Canadian citizen on December 15, 2025, when Bill C-3 — the Act to Amend the Citizenship Act — came into full effect, ending decades of exclusion for families born across multiple generations outside the country.

**What changed under Bill C-3:**
On December 15, 2025, Bill C-3 came into force, amending the Canadian Citizenship Act to no longer limit citizenship by descent to the first generation born abroad. The new legislation retroactively restores citizenship to 'Lost Canadians' and grants automatic citizenship to anyone born abroad to a Canadian parent before December 15, 2025. For children born *after* that date, Bill C-3 establishes a Substantial Connection test, requiring a Canadian parent to have spent at least 1,095 cumulative days — three years — physically present in Canada before their child's birth or adoption.

**Why the law had to change:**
Bill C-3 was introduced in response to a constitutional challenge in Bjorkquist v. Canada (2023 ONSC 7152), in which the Ontario Superior Court found the first-generation limit on citizenship by descent to be unconstitutional. The Government of Canada did not appeal the ruling, as it agreed the law had unacceptable outcomes for children of Canadians who were born outside the country. This created the class of 'Lost Canadians' — descendants of Canadian citizens who, through no fault of their own, were cut off from their birthright because their Canadian parents had also been born abroad.

**What to watch next:**
For individuals with Canadian ancestry born abroad, these changes may restore or newly confer citizenship rights, and those who believe they may qualify should seek confirmation through a citizenship certificate application.
